chapter: Bird's world, singers and the new music
title: Freddie Webster's 'Stardust' and sound
summary: He credits Webster as the real 'Stardust' player, with an unmatched sound.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Talking about trumpet players in that time, what do you remember about Freddie Webster?

Well, I heard Freddie Webster play "Stardust," and I really didn't want to play "Stardust" no more after I heard that -- just to let you know what I thought about how he was playing. But I really didn't want to play "Stardust" no more after I heard him play it. Butt I had to, because I had played it first, which got out there before his solo did -- and everybody was giving me credit for playing "Stardust." But Freddie Webster was the man that really played "Stardust." I don't take nothing away from Freddie Webster. In fact, Freddie Webster played tremendous everything. Too bad he had to go away on
But how do you think he got that kind of a sound?

I don't know how he got it. But whichever way he developed it, he sure had it. I can say that. He had a beautiful sound. I don't know how he got that. Louis didn't have it, and nobody else... Dizzy didn't have it. But Freddie had it, and he could make everybody sound bad, because all he had to do was play the melody, and everybody would say, 'Gee, leave(?) this at that.' Even with Dizzy, he sounded like a toy trumpet compared to Freddie Webster. Freddie was something else.
